messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 34

At twenty-seven, they speak with the steady, practiced tone of someone used to calming other people. As a special education teacher, they spend their days breaking tasks into manageable steps, noticing small changes in mood, keeping their classroom predictable and safe. When they talk about what happened, that same carefulness is there, but it is strained, as if every sentence has to pass through a tight gate.

The stalking begins in a way they first try to make ordinary. A parent volunteer at a community event starts lingering after conversations, then sends a message through social media saying it was nice to meet them. They reply politely once and think little of it. Over the next few weeks, the messages multiply. At first they are familiar rather than threatening—comments about their smile, about seeing them at the grocery store, about what time they usually leave school. Reading that last message, they remember a cold drop in their stomach. They tell themself there must be some harmless explanation. They are good at de-escalating, at giving people the benefit of the doubt.

But the contact continues after they stop responding. Flowers are left on their car in the school parking lot. A note appears under the windshield wiper, written as if the sender knows them intimately. Then they begin noticing the same car on their street in the evenings. Once, while walking home, they hear footsteps behind them and turn to see the same person from the community event standing across the road, watching. They do not approach, do not speak, only stare long enough that the patient feels pinned in place. After that, fear moves into their life with a permanence that surprises them.

They change routines first. They leave school by different exits, ask a colleague to walk them to their car, scan windows before entering their apartment. Their partner wants them to stay elsewhere for a while, but they resist because they do not want their whole life rearranged by someone else's obsession. Still, they begin sleeping with a chair pushed against the front door. Every noise in the hallway jolts them upright. In the dark, their mind runs through images of the stalker outside the apartment, at the school gates, stepping out from behind their car. They know these thoughts are repetitive, but they cannot stop rehearsing them.

At work, the impact shows in ways that trouble them deeply. They have always taken pride in being patient and emotionally available with their students, especially when routines change or behavior escalates. Now, when an unexpected knock comes at the classroom door, their whole body flinches. If a parent arrives unannounced, they feel heat rush through their chest and have to look down at their lesson plan to keep their face neutral. They become more rigid about classroom procedures, checking the locked door several times a day, watching the corridor through the narrow glass panel. They hate that their students notice. One child asks why they keep looking outside. They laugh it off, then go to the staff bathroom and cry quietly, ashamed that their fear has followed them into a room that is supposed to feel safe for children.

Their partner becomes both a comfort and a witness to the ways they have changed. Before, they liked evening walks, busy cafés, spontaneous plans. Now they want curtains closed before sunset. They ask their partner to text when they arrive anywhere, and if a message is delayed, irritation quickly gives way to panic. They start arguments about locks, about who might have seen them, about whether posting a photo online is dangerous. Later they apologize, saying they know they sound controlling, but in the moment it feels like survival. Intimacy becomes harder too. If their partner touches them unexpectedly from behind in the kitchen, they jerk away before they can think. They see hurt flash across their partner’s face and feel grief on top of fear.

Even after the stalking is formally reported and the visible contact decreases, their body does not seem to believe the danger has passed. They still scan parking lots and reflective shop windows. They memorize number plates without meaning to. They wake from dreams in which they are trying to lock a door that will not close, or trying to call for help without a voice. On weekends, they sometimes lose hours sitting on the couch, phone in hand, rereading old messages as if studying them might finally make the whole experience coherent. Other times they avoid anything that reminds them of it, refusing to go near the street where they were followed, deleting apps, asking friends not to mention the case.

They describe feeling split between the person they were and the person they are now. In the classroom, they can still be warm, creative, funny; they can still kneel beside a student and celebrate a small success with genuine joy. But underneath runs a near-constant calculation of risk. They miss the ease they once had in public, the assumption that ordinary life was not a stage on which they were being watched. What unsettles them most is not only what the stalker did, but how thoroughly that fear has taught their mind and body to expect intrusion, even in moments that should belong only to them.
